title: Clients, pricing and a UI portfolio that proves your craft

say: Clients, pricing and a UI portfolio that proves your craft.
This is the video for module three of UI Design with Figma.
Most UI projects that go wrong were unclear from the first conversation. A client says I need an app design, and means something very different from what you imagine.

panel.heading: Most projects go wrong on day one
items: I need an app design means many things

say: Discovery is a short, structured call that turns a vague request into a defined list of screens and deliverables you can price.

panel.heading: Most projects go wrong on day one
items: I need an app design means many things

say: Ask about brand: is there a logo, colours, fonts? And users: what are the three most important things they do, and has anyone mapped the flows?

panel.heading: Five areas to ask about
items: Users and flows: top three tasks
Content: who writes text, real photos
Build: who develops it, with what

say: Ask which platforms and phones, and who supplies the text and photos.

panel.heading: Five areas to ask about
items: Users and flows: top three tasks
Content: who writes text, real photos
Build: who develops it, with what

say: Ask who is building it and with what. Also ask for one decision-maker and one combined list of comments per round.

panel.heading: Five areas to ask about
items: Users and flows: top three tasks
Content: who writes text, real photos
Build: who develops it, with what

say: For example, Kemi runs a tailoring studio in Ibadan and wants an Android app. She has a logo and two colours, but no wireframes. So the quote must include simple user flows first.

panel.heading: From a call to a screen inventory

say: Her three tasks become 10 screens, plus 4 state frames, like an empty orders list and a booking slot unavailable.

panel.heading: From a call to a screen inventory

say: The inventory lists 7 components, and a spec page for handoff, because her developer has no paid Figma seat.

panel.heading: From a call to a screen inventory

say: Send a one-page summary the same day and ask the client to confirm it before any quote.

panel.heading: From a call to a screen inventory
panel.rule: Confirm the screen inventory in writing before you quote.

say: Watch for red flags. Make it like a big company's app means dozens of screens, so ask which three matter most. Content later means sample content, with replacing it as a separate task.
Each extra platform multiplies screens. A logo is a separate project. And no named decision-maker means endless feedback, unless you set limits.

panel.heading: Hidden scope to price separately
items: Just make it like a big company's app
We will send the content later
Can you also do the logo?

say: Weight each screen by effort. As a starting scale, a simple screen is about 3 hours, a medium one about 5, and a complex form or checkout about 8. Track your own time to make these honest.

panel.heading: Build the estimate from the screens

say: Then add the work that is not screens: foundations and components, the prototype, and handoff.

panel.heading: Build the estimate from the screens

say: Add a buffer for unknowns. Kemi's app comes to 91 hours, plus 15 percent, about 105 hours.

panel.heading: Build the estimate from the screens

say: At an example rate of 10,000 naira an hour, 105 hours is 1,050,000 naira. Set your own rate from your costs, skill and local demand.

card.title: Payments tied to milestones
card.note: Illustrative naira rate, not a market figure.

say: Split it by milestone: a 50 percent deposit of 525,000 naira, 30 percent when key screens are approved, and 20 percent at handoff.

card.title: Payments tied to milestones
card.note: Illustrative naira rate, not a market figure.

say: Write the limits too: two rounds of feedback per stage, and a price for each new screen. A new medium screen here is 50,000 naira. If the client wants to save money, remove a line, not just the total.

card.title: Payments tied to milestones
card.note: Illustrative naira rate, not a market figure.

say: Protect your money. Be wary of a new client who sends more than agreed and asks you to refund the difference.

panel.heading: Scams aimed at freelancers

cards.d: A client sends more than agreed and asks for a refund. Be wary.
A screenshot or SMS alert is not money. Confirm it in your bank or wallet app.
Never share your BVN, OTPs or PIN. Share view-only links until final payment.

say: A payment screenshot or SMS alert is not money. Confirm every payment inside your own bank or wallet app before you start or deliver.

say: Never share your BVN, OTPs or banking PIN. And keep the file in your own Figma team, sharing view-only links, until the final payment.

say: Reviewers look past the final screens to see how you work. Do screens use component instances? Are colours linked to styles, not loose hex values?

panel.heading: What reviewers check in your file
items: Colours and text linked to styles
A prototype with no dead ends

say: Are layers named, and are states designed beyond the happy path? Does the prototype run without dead ends?
So show two or three projects in depth, with one honest case study. If it is a practice concept, say so.

panel.heading: What reviewers check in your file
items: Colours and text linked to styles
A prototype with no dead ends

say: To remember. Run discovery across five areas, and confirm the screen inventory in writing.
Build prices from weighted screens, stage the payments, and confirm money in your own account.
Then pick one target path and act on it every week for 90 days.

panel.heading: Remember
items: Discovery: brand, users, platform, content, build
Confirm the screen inventory in writing
Weight screens; price extras as lines
Stage payments; confirm in your own account
Show the system behind the screens

say: Now practise. Run a practice discovery call, write a priced proposal with staged payments, and publish your first case study with a view-only Figma link.
